content: Desonide is a corticosteroid approved by the FDA for the treatment of inflammatory and pruritic manifestations of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses. Common adverse reactions include contact dermatitis, dry skin, pruritus, stinging, burning sensation, and irritation. For adults, Desonide cream or ointment should be applied as a thin film to the affected areas two to four times daily, depending on the severity of the condition. Therapy should be discontinued once control is achieved. If no improvement is observed within two weeks, the diagnosis should be reassessed. Desonide should not be used with occlusive dressings. There is limited information regarding off-label use of Desonide in adults and pediatric patients. Safety and effectiveness in pediatric patients have not been established. Pediatric patients are at greater risk of hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis suppression and Cushing's syndrome due to their larger skin surface area-to-body mass ratio. Adverse effects such as striae, growth retardation, delayed weight gain, and intracranial hypertension have been reported in children treated with topical corticosteroids. Desonide is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to any of its components. Systemic absorption of topical corticosteroids can lead to reversible HPA axis suppression, Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, and glucosuria. Patients applying Desonide to large surface areas or under occlusion should be periodically evaluated for HPA axis suppression. If suppression occurs, the drug should be withdrawn, application frequency reduced, or a less potent corticosteroid substituted. Recovery of HPA axis function is generally prompt upon discontinuation. Desonide should not be used in the presence of skin infections unless appropriate antifungal or antibacterial agents are also used. If irritation or allergic contact dermatitis develops, Desonide should be discontinued, and appropriate therapy should be initiated. It should not be used in the eyes or on infected or atrophic skin. During pregnancy, Desonide should only be used if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. It is not known whether Desonide is excreted in human milk following topical application, so caution should be exercised when administered to nursing mothers. Desonide has anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive properties. Its mechanism of action is thought to involve the induction of phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins, which control the biosynthesis of inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes by inhibiting the release of arachidonic acid. Desonide is supplied as a cream or ointment containing 0.05% of the active ingredient. It should be stored at 20°-25°C (68°-77°F) and protected from freezing. Patients should use Desonide as directed by their physician, avoid contact with the eyes, and report any signs of local adverse reactions. The treated area should not be occluded unless directed by a physician. There is no established interaction between alcohol and Desonide. Patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of alcohol consumption while using this medication. Desonide is marketed under brand names such as Desowen, LoKara, Tridesilon, Verdeso, and Desonate.
